parsed.title: I AM: The Root Speaks — Full Draft
parsed.summary: This paper argues that if God is the ultimate root of reality, the central question is not merely whether humans can reason upward to Him, but whether He has spoken. It presents the biblical claim that God discloses Himself—naming Himself 'I AM WHO I AM' to Moses, and in Christ taking that divine identity into history. The paper distinguishes discovery (what the world requires) from disclosure (whom God says He is), and argues that Christianity is built not only on inference but on God's self-revelation, which must be received rather than merely deduced.

atoms.name: The Root Speaks
atoms.statementTechnical: Christianity does not merely claim that God can be inferred; it claims that God has disclosed Himself.
atoms.statementPlain: Christianity says God has actually spoken and shown us who He is, not just that we can figure Him out by reasoning.
atoms.falsificationCondition: If Christianity's authoritative texts and central tradition did not claim divine self-disclosure, or if the claim that God has spoken were shown to be a later invention with no basis in the earliest Christian movement, this claim would be falsified.
atoms.notes: This is the central claim of the paper, stated in the [!claim] callout at P79.

atoms.name: The Divine Name as Boundary
atoms.statementTechnical: The name 'I AM WHO I AM' (Exodus 3:14) functions as a boundary that prevents God from being defined by anything more ultimate than Himself; it names God from the side of His own self-existent existence.
atoms.statementPlain: When God says 'I AM WHO I AM,' He is not giving a label like other names. He is saying He cannot be defined by anything deeper or larger—He is the root, not a thing among things.
atoms.falsificationCondition: If Exodus 3:14 could be shown to be a creaturely label that places God within a larger category, or if the text's grammar and context clearly indicate God is being named by comparison to other beings, this claim would be falsified.
atoms.notes: Based on Exodus 3:14 and the surrounding argument in P12–P26.

atoms.name: Jesus Takes the Divine Name
atoms.statementTechnical: In John's Gospel, Jesus applies the 'I am' formula to Himself with predicates that identify Him with the divine root, not merely as a teacher or prophet.
atoms.statementPlain: Jesus doesn't just talk about God—He says things like 'I am the bread of life' and 'I am the truth,' using the same 'I am' language God used for Himself. That's identity language, not just religious advice.
atoms.falsificationCondition: If the Johannine 'I am' sayings could be shown to be later theological additions with no historical connection to Jesus, or if they functioned merely as ordinary metaphors without identity claims, this claim would be falsified.
atoms.notes: Based on the list of 'I am' sayings in John's Gospel (P42–P53).

atoms.name: Disclosure and Discovery Are Distinct but Convergent
atoms.statementTechnical: Discovery asks what the world requires; disclosure asks whom God says He is. These are distinct epistemic routes that should converge without being collapsed into one method.
atoms.statementPlain: We can study the world to learn about God (discovery), and we can listen to what God says about Himself (disclosure). They are different, but they should fit together.
atoms.falsificationCondition: If discovery and disclosure were shown to be mutually exclusive or contradictory, or if one method consistently yielded results incompatible with the other, this claim would be falsified.
atoms.notes: Stated in the [!bridge] callout at P38 and developed in P28–P37.

atoms.name: Christianity Is Built on Disclosure, Not Only Inference
atoms.statementTechnical: Christianity is not built only on upward inference from effects to cause; it is built on God's self-disclosure in speech, action, covenant, and ultimately in Christ.
atoms.statementPlain: Christianity doesn't just rely on arguments from the world to God. It relies on God actually speaking, acting, making promises, and coming into history.
atoms.falsificationCondition: If Christianity's foundational documents and earliest traditions did not center on divine self-disclosure but only on human inference, or if the disclosure events (e.g., Exodus, Incarnation) were shown to be unhistorical, this claim would be falsified.

atoms.name: The Disclosed Portrait Can Be Stated Before It Is Proven
atoms.statementTechnical: The Christian portrait of God—self-existent, non-derived, personal, speaking, faithful, and revealed in Christ—can be stated honestly as a claim before it is publicly proven, and then tested for convergence with reality, reason, history, and experience.
atoms.statementPlain: We can describe what Christianity says about God without first proving it. Then we can ask whether the world, our reasoning, history, and our experience line up with that description.
atoms.falsificationCondition: If the disclosed portrait were incoherent or could not be stated without presupposing its own truth, or if no possible convergence test could be formulated, this claim would be falsified.

atoms.name: Disclosure and Discovery Bridge
atoms.statementTechnical: Discovery asks what the world requires; disclosure asks whom God says He is.
atoms.statementPlain: Discovery is about what the world needs to be explained; disclosure is about who God says He is.

atoms.name: Exodus 3:14 — I AM WHO I AM
atoms.statementTechnical: Exodus 3:14 records God's self-naming to Moses as 'I AM WHO I AM.'
atoms.statementPlain: In Exodus 3:14, God tells Moses His name is 'I AM WHO I AM.'
atoms.notes: Scripture citation used as evidence for the claim about the divine name.

atoms.name: Johannine 'I Am' Sayings
atoms.statementTechnical: The Gospel of John records Jesus using 'I am' with predicates such as bread of life, light of the world, door, good shepherd, resurrection and life, way/truth/life, and true vine.
atoms.statementPlain: In John's Gospel, Jesus says things like 'I am the bread of life' and 'I am the way, the truth, and the life.'

atoms.name: The Skeptic's Objection
atoms.statementTechnical: A skeptic does not have to accept the Bible's authority to understand the paper's project; the paper is not arguing 'Exodus 3:14 is in the Bible, therefore God exists.'
atoms.statementPlain: You don't have to believe the Bible to follow what this paper is saying. It's not saying 'the Bible says it, so it's true.'

atoms.name: Revelation Can Be Misunderstood or False
atoms.statementTechnical: Revelation can be misunderstood, claims of revelation can be false, Scripture must be interpreted, history must be investigated, and the Church can mishandle what it receives.
atoms.statementPlain: People can misunderstand revelation, false claims of revelation exist, the Bible needs interpretation, history needs checking, and the Church can get it wrong.

atoms.name: Convergence of Reason and Revelation
atoms.statementTechnical: If Christianity is true, reality, reason, history, and experience will converge with the disclosed portrait of God.
atoms.statementPlain: If Christianity is true, then what we find in the world, in logic, in history, and in our lives should fit with the God it describes.

atoms.name: Has God Spoken?
atoms.statementTechnical: If God is the root, the first problem is not only whether we can reach Him, but whether He has spoken.
atoms.statementPlain: If God is the ultimate source, the big question isn't just whether we can find Him—it's whether He has spoken.
atoms.notes: Opening question of the paper, P02–P03.

atoms.name: The Child and the Father Analogy
atoms.statementTechnical: A child can learn about his father by studying the house the father built or by hearing the father speak; these are not enemies.
atoms.statementPlain: A kid can learn about his dad by looking at the house he built or by listening to him talk. Both are valid.
atoms.notes: Analogy in P30–P34, used to illustrate discovery and disclosure.
